transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton.
President Trump says the U.S. will obtain diesel fuel from Russia, relaxing years of
U.S. pressure on Moscow to combat prices ahead of midterms.
Trump said on social media that he struck the deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin
in a phone call.
The announcement comes after President Trump signed a sweeping sanctions law against Russia
last month to clamp down on Russia's energy economy over the Ukraine war.
Hours after an international humanitarian legal expert was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize,
the State Department announced sanctions on the International Criminal Court.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio has vowed to dismantle the world's only standing war
crimes tribunal, as NPR's Michelle Kellerman reports.
Secretary Rubio says the U.S. will ban transactions with what he calls a "rogue court," cutting
off its resources and crippling its ability to operate.
America never joined the court.
We don't need that court, and we don't want it.
The ICC was set up as a court of last resort for victims of war crimes, crimes against
humanity and genocide.
The U.S. protested an investigation into Afghanistan, which could have implicated U.S. service members.
The ICC closed that investigation.
The U.S. also opposes the arrest warrant against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over
the war in Gaza.
The ICC says in a statement that it will not be deterred, but its fate now rests in the
hands of the states that created it.
Michelle Kellerman, NPR News, Washington.
President Trump has picked conservative commentator Katie Zaccaria to be his new White House press
secretary.
It comes after the departure of Caroline Levitt in August.
Zaccaria has been an adviser for Trump's truth social platform and briefly served as
a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security.
Hurricane Isaias is forecast to make landfall tonight on the northern Gulf Coast, and PR's
Debbie Elliott reports it's now a powerful Category 3 hurricane with 115-mile-an-hour
winds.
National Hurricane Center director Michael Brennan says Isaias is on track to hit northwest
Florida.
This powerful hurricane expected to make landfall this evening into the late night hours and
then move quickly inland across portions of the Florida Panhandle and up into Alabama
as we go through the overnight hours into Saturday.
He says hazards will be a storm surge of six to nine feet, damaging winds, and rainfall
up to 15 inches.
Brennan says expect widespread power outages, tornadoes, and flash flooding as the storm
moves inland over the southeastern U.S.
Isaias is the first hurricane of the Atlantic season, which has until now been dampened by
a strong El Nino weather pattern.
Debbie Elliott, NPR News, Crestview, Florida.
Isaias headed by someone aged 75 or older are now America's wealthiest, while the youngest
families saw their wealth decline in the past three years.
That's according to the Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances.
It underscores how robust stock market gains have made wealthy American families even richer.
This is NPR News.
Senior ICE official Marcos Charles says federal officers shot and wounded a Dominican man
in New York because they believed their lives were in danger.
Police officers shot 28-year-old Oscar Belgaal in the neck yesterday while he was driving
with his five-year-old son.
DHS says the officers didn't see the child.
Kenyan health officials are on guard after a man with Ebola returned home from the Democratic
Republic of Congo and died last week.
NPR's Jonathan Lambert reports no one he came in contact with has tested positive.
The death marks Kenya's first Ebola case of this outbreak, which is now the second largest
ever.
At our sea, more than 8,700 people have gotten sick, and over 4,200 have died since May.
Official case counts have declined somewhat over the past two weeks as previous hotspots
of the disease cooled down.
But health officials caution this decline might be misleading since the outbreak has spread
to more areas with ongoing conflict.
Some aspects of the response are improving.
Health officials are reaching about 19 contacts per case, up from about 10 in the early days.
But that's still not high enough, officials say, roughly 70 percent of deaths are still
occurring outside of clinics, suggesting the response isn't meeting those who need it most.
Jonathan Lambert, NPR News.
Alaska Pollock.
The fish in most fish sticks and imitation crab is at the center of a political and cultural
fight over industrial trawling in Alaska.
The nets for Alaska's massive pollock fishery also catch salmon and other marine life as
salmon runs collapse across western Alaska indigenous communities and smaller commercial
fishers say they're bearing the costs.
I'm Rylan Barton.
You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
